keyPoints: Connect workload to constrained resources
A busy CPU is an observation. Compare demand, run queue, memory pressure and service latency before choosing a repair.
slides.narration:
A server feels slow, and the first visible process uses a large amount of memory. Killing it seems decisive, but the process may be the database doing legitimate work while the real problem is a saturated storage path. Resource management requires identifying what is running, what it is waiting for, and which limit actually constrains the workload.

This chapter distinguishes process identity, scheduling, memory accounting, signals, and resource boundaries. Observation comes before termination. A process is part of a service lifecycle, not merely a row to remove from a screen.

slides.title: 7.1 Programs vs. Processes
keyPoints: Linux example — 7.1
Compare the executable name with a running instance.
What to check: The file is a program; the shell PID identifies a process executing it.
slides.narration:
A program is executable code stored or otherwise available for execution. A process is a running instance with its own identity, address space, open file descriptors, credentials, and execution state. Many processes can run the same program with different arguments and permissions.

A service may consist of one process, a parent and several workers, or a collection of cooperating programs. Killing one worker may cause the supervisor to replace it immediately. That is not evidence that kill failed; it may be the intended lifecycle policy.

Identify the owning service before acting. The service manager often knows which processes belong together and how to stop them cleanly. Stopping a service through its supervisor is usually safer than guessing which PID represents the whole application.

slides.title: 7.2 Process IDs
keyPoints: A process ID, or PID, identifies a process within a PID namespace. PIDs are reused after processes exit. A number copied from an old incident note is therefore not a durable identity.
$$ expands to the shell’s PID in the usual interactive context. The elapsed time and command help establish which process is actually being inspected.
Linux example — 7.2
slides.narration:
A process ID, or PID, identifies a process within a PID namespace. PIDs are reused after processes exit. A number copied from an old incident note is therefore not a durable identity.

$$ expands to the shell’s PID in the usual interactive context. The elapsed time and command help establish which process is actually being inspected.

Before signaling a process, confirm its current executable, owner, start time, and relationship to the service. A separate check followed by a later signal still has a race if the process exits and the PID is reused. Service-manager operations and newer process-handle interfaces can reduce ambiguity. Avoid building critical automation around stale PID files alone.

slides.title: 7.3 Parent and Child Processes
keyPoints: A process can create child processes. The parent PID, or PPID, records a relationship useful for understanding shells, workers, and supervisors. A child can outlive its original parent and be adopted by an appropriate reaper or subreaper.
The process tree reveals relationships, but it does not by itself describe every service boundary. A service’s control group can include processes whose ancestry has changed.
Linux example — 7.3
slides.narration:
A process can create child processes. The parent PID, or PPID, records a relationship useful for understanding shells, workers, and supervisors. A child can outlive its original parent and be adopted by an appropriate reaper or subreaper.

The process tree reveals relationships, but it does not by itself describe every service boundary. A service’s control group can include processes whose ancestry has changed.

After a child exits, its parent ordinarily collects its termination status through a wait operation. Failing to do so creates a zombie entry, discussed later. Good process supervision includes starting, signaling, collecting exit status, and deciding whether restart is appropriate.

slides.title: 7.6 Foreground and Background Jobs
keyPoints: A foreground job interacts with the terminal normally. Appending & starts a command asynchronously and returns the shell prompt. Bash assigns a job number distinct from the operating-system PID.

$! captures the PID associated with the most recent asynchronous command. fg returns a job to the foreground; bg resumes a stopped job in the background. These are shell job-control operations, not service-management commands.
Linux example — 7.6
slides.narration:

$! captures the PID associated with the most recent asynchronous command. fg returns a job to the foreground; bg resumes a stopped job in the background. These are shell job-control operations, not service-management commands.

Backgrounding a command does not make it a reliable daemon. It may depend on the session, terminal, environment, or working directory. Use a terminal multiplexer for interactive continuity and a supervisor such as systemd for an actual service with restart and logging requirements.

A signal notifies a process of an event or requests an action. SIGTERM asks for termination and can be handled for cleanup. SIGINT commonly corresponds to an interactive interrupt. slides.title: 7.9 Process Priorities
keyPoints: Scheduling priority influences how runnable work competes for CPU time. It does not manufacture CPU capacity and does not resolve every performance problem. A process blocked on storage may gain little from a CPU-priority change.
Linux example — 7.9

slides.narration:
Scheduling priority influences how runnable work competes for CPU time. It does not manufacture CPU capacity and does not resolve every performance problem. A process blocked on storage may gain little from a CPU-priority change.

Ordinary Linux scheduling and real-time scheduling have different policies. Raising a process into a real-time class without understanding its behavior can starve important system work. Do not treat real-time priority as a generic performance switch.

Measure the actual bottleneck first. For background maintenance, reducing scheduling preference may be appropriate when it protects interactive service latency. Even then, the job can still compete for memory and I/O, so CPU priority is only one part of resource control.

slides.narration:
CPU utilization describes how processor time is being spent. Distinguish user-space work, kernel work, idle time, and other reported categories. A busy CPU can indicate productive work, an inefficient loop, encryption, interrupt load, or many other causes.

A machine with eight logical CPUs can have one saturated application thread while the overall CPU average remains modest. Conversely, a high aggregate percentage can be acceptable when latency targets are met and the workload is intentionally batch-oriented.

Use interval measurements and thread-level evidence when appropriate. Compare against the service’s throughput and response time. “CPU is 100%” is incomplete until you state which CPU or process, over what interval, and whether useful work is progressing.

slides.title: 7.17 Control Groups
keyPoints: Linux example — 7.17
Inspect this process's cgroup placement.
What to check: A cgroup path locates the policy scope; inspect that scope's controls before drawing conclusions.
slides.narration:
Control groups, or cgroups, organize processes for resource accounting and control. They can constrain CPU, memory, process counts, and I/O according to available controllers. systemd uses cgroups to group service processes and apply policy.

Cgroup v2 presents a unified hierarchy with controller-specific interfaces. A limit is meaningful only when the relevant controller and hierarchy support it. Do not blindly write values into /sys/fs/cgroup on a system managed by another owner.

Use systemd properties such as MemoryMax=, CPUQuota=, and TasksMax= for managed services when appropriate. A quota limits available CPU time; a weight influences relative competition. Neither is a substitute for understanding workload requirements. Test throttling and failure behavior before applying limits to production. (R16)
